claims.text: With the smallest flowers in subg. Visciramosae, Moraea inconspicua is distinguished by its flowers with fully reflexed tepals, the outer mostly 12-18 mm long (rarely up to 25 mm), the limb at least twice as long as the claw. In addition the rhipidial spathes are short, usually less than 28 mm long and sometimes only 18 mm. Flower colour is variable, mostly yellow or partly to completely brown, but white-flowered morphs occur in the Biedouw Valley near Clanwilliam and on the Agulhas Plain near Elim, the latter with the smallest flowers recorded in the species. In Namaqualand flowers are sometimes ivory-coloured or pink, but also yellow or brown as elsewhere. The foliage leaves are usually straight and erect below but often trailing distally, and have channelled blades, but plants from Namaqualand have distinctive spirally coiled leaves with a plane surface and on this basis have been segregated as subsp. namaquensis. Populations from the northern Cederberg and Biedouw Valley have unusually large flowers for the species, the outer tepals up to 25 mm long, thus matching those of closely allied M. bituminosa. The narrow leaves, short style crests and almost fully reflexed tepal limbs conform to M. inconspicua. Superficially similar Moraea viscaria, is a white-flowered species with spreading tepals 15-23 mm long, a strong floral odour, and relatively well-developed style crests up to 6 mm long, half as long to ± as long as the style branches. Moraea saldanhensis may also be confused with M. inconspicua but has slate-blue flowers with the tepal claws as long as to slightly longer than the limbs, the latter usually reflexed to ± 45º.

claims.text: Moraea incurva has blue to violet flowers with the inner tepals either 3-lobed with the inner lobe linear and 18-20 mm long, or entire and thus exceptional but not unknown in subg. Vieusseuxia. The inner tepal limbs are abruptly curved inward (hence the name incurva) on suberect claws. The species otherwise conforms to subg. Vieusseuxia in the solitary basal leaf, modest size of the flowers, and in the filaments united in a slender column with only the tips free. The filament column, 10-11 mm long, raises the anthers above the bases of the inner tepal limbs and the orange anthers are thus prominently displayed. The immediate relationships of M. incurva are uncertain but molecular studies place it close to M. unguiculata and M. tripetala. The entire to 3-lobed inner tepals with incurved limbs and long filament column recall M. barkerae and the two species may be, on this basis, closely related.

claims.text: Distinctive in having several foliage leaves, all inserted well above the ground just below the first branch, large yellow flowers with bright red anthers that extend beyond the stigmas, and nodding capsules. The large corms of M. indecora are particularly deep seated, buried at least 200 mm below the ground, partly wedged in bed rock. Moraea (x = 10) but at least M. papilionacea (n = 9 and 8) also departs from that base number.

claims.text: With its open, poppy-like flowers, either bright orange-red or creamy green with a brown centre, Moraea insolens is one of the most striking species in the genus. The filaments are united in a smooth, dark brown column and the large anthers, ± 8 mm long are closely appressed to and exceed the narrow style branches with their tiny crests. The inner tepals closely resemble the outer in colour and orientation and are only slightly smaller. Moraea insolens is probably most closely related to M. lurida, a species of sandstone soils which usually has dark maroon flowers, sometimes with contrasting white markings, and similarly reduced style branches and crests but smaller inner tepals often with 3-lobed limbs. The two species share an unusual karyotype, unique in sect. Vieusseuxia.

claims.text: The asymmetric corm with brown, ± woody corm tunics, relatively blunt, brown-tipped rhipidial spathes, and yellow, darkly veined tepals place Moraea intermedia in subg. Umbellatae. The long basal internode with leaves clustered at the first aerial node recalls M. nana of the subgenus, but the flowers have typical Moraea-like style branches with terminal, transverse stigma lobes and prominent, paired petaloid style crests. Unlike the typical Moraea flower, however, all six tepals of M. intermedia have short claws clasping the base of the filament column, the claws all bearing basal nectaries, and the limbs each have a nectar guide at the base. Other Moraea-type flowers have inner tepals lacking both nectaries and nectar guides. The similarly marked inner and outer tepals recall the Homeria-type flower as found in subg. Umbellatae in M. maximiliani and M. umbellata, whereas M. cooperi, M. linderi, M. longiflora and M. margaretae have more-or-less typical Moraea-type flowers. The remaining member of the alliance, M. nana, has spreading, subequal tepals with short claws clasping the base of the filament column but the style branches are reduced to paired filiform arms extending between the anthers. At the type locality, Moraea intermedia is parapatric with the closely related M. margaretae, which favours somewhat wetter sites, and a range of hybrids between the two species occurs there.

claims.text: Moraea kamiesmontana stands out in subg. Galaxia not only in its particularly small size but in the structure of its flowers. In other species of the subgenus the flowers have flaccid, widely cupped tepals that lack distinct claws, but in M. kamiesmontana the ascending tepal claws form a narrow cup enclosing the filaments and the limbs are sharply flexed at right angles to the cup, thus extended horizontally. The chromosome number, 2n = 18, is the ancestral number for the subgenus, and we interpret Moraea kamiesmontana as a relict species, surviving in specialised, seasonally moist, montane habitats.

claims.text: Broadly resembling the more common Moraea miniata, M. karooica may differ in leaf number, usually single (rarely two or three) vs. two or three in M. miniata, but more fundamentally in the flowers. Moraea karooica has ascending tepal claws that together form a shallow cup and a cylindric filament column, whereas in M. miniata the short tepal claws clasp the base of the bulbous filament column. Moraea karooica may be most closely allied to the rare M. fenestrata of the Tanqua Basin, which has a similar habit but consistently two or more leaves, and tepals conspicuously narrowed at the base, thus usually forming a windowed cup. Populations of M. karooica with more than one leaf are from the Koedoes Mtns and Verlatenkloof near Sutherland.

claims.text: Typically has slightly twisted leaves with undulate margins, and the outer inflorescence spathes are free distally and curve outward. claims.text: Plants 160-350 mm high. Corm ± conical, 12-18 mm at widest diam., with numerous small cormlets round base; tunics of medium-textured, matted, dark grey fibres. Stem flexuose, 1- to 5-branched, rarely simple, bearing sheathing leaves 32-38 mm long. Foliage leaf solitary, linear, longer than stem, erect to falcate, narrowly channelled, 2-3 mm wide opened flat. Rhipidial spathes with brown, attenuate tips, inner 33-45 mm long, outer ± half as long. Flowers fugaceous, blue, outer tepal limbs with white nectar guides at bases sometimes edged with dark blue, limbs of both whorls ± half reflexed, inner often more so than outer, unscented; outer tepals ± lanceolate, 22-27 x 8-9 mm, limbs 15-18 mm long, claws 7-8 mm long, inner tepals 17-20 x 5-7 mm. Filaments ± 8 mm long, united in lower half; anthers ± 5 mm long, grey-blue; pollen white or pale blue. Ovary ± cylindric, 5-6 mm long; style branches ± 7 x 5 mm, crests narrowly wedge-shaped, 7-8 mm long. Capsules and seeds unknown.

claims.text: Resembling a second Little Karoo species, Moraea exiliflora, also with a solitary, narrowly channelled basal leaf, M. lazulina has significantly larger flowers and is typically a taller plant, usually with a moderately branched stem. The flowers are always blue with large, white nectar guides on the outer tepals, 22-27 x 8-9 mm, whereas Moraea exiliflora has smaller, pale blue, mauve or white flowers with yellow (or white) nectar guides and outer tepals 14-17 x 4.5-6.0 mm. Other features of M. lazulina are likewise larger than in M. exiliflora. The shape of the flowers also differs to some extent, the tepal limbs of M. lazulina being reflexed more than 45º, the inner sometimes more so than the outer whereas the tepal limbs of M. exiliflora are laxly spreading to reflexed up to 30º.

claims.text: Recognised by the pink to lilac flowers with outer tepals 27-30 mm long, and 3-lobed inner tepals 16-18 mm long. The inner tepals have a narrow, channelled claw but the 3-lobed limb consists of an erect central cusp ± 9 mm long and shorter rounded lateral lobes. The filaments are 7-8 mm long with a papillate or smooth column, The species is clearly allied to the widespread southern African winter-rainfall M. unguiculata, a remarkably variable species, both as regards perianth colour and size, but its critical features are inner tepals 10-12 mm long and trilobed with the central cusp linear and coiled inward, filaments usually 3-5 mm long with the column lightly to densely papillate, and the outer tepals are typically 12-16 mm long, rarely up to 24 mm long in northern Namaqualand populations. The stems in M. unguiculata are almost always branched unless depauperate due to environmental conditions but typically unbranched in M. lilacina. The outer tepals of M. unguiculata may be white to cream-coloured, brown, violet, or even dull yellow and usually have a contrasting mark at the base of the limb, and the style branches are narrow and spreading as in M. lilacina, but with erect crests 2.0-4.0(-5.5) mm long vs. 5-8 mm in M. lilacina.

claims.text: Particularly tall for sect. Hexaglottis and standing up to 2 m high, Moraea longifolia is distinguished by the pale yellow flowers with faint nectar guides without dark spotting, comparatively short style branches, 4-6 mm long, and large, obovoid to club-shaped capsules. Moraea longifolia is tetraploid and known to be self-compatible and autogamous, whereas the other species of the section are diploid and self-incompatible (compatibility relations are not known for M. brevituba). Closely related and similar M. lewisiae has cylindric 3-lobed capsules, slightly larger, deeper yellow flowers with prominently spotted nectar guides, and style branches 6-7 mm long. Also sometimes confused with M. longifolia, M. riparia has smaller capsules and bright yellow, strongly scented flowers, and is self-incompatible.

claims.text: Specialised in subg. Homeria in having the branches of the style almost or entirely suppressed, the style either dividing near the apex of the anthers, with very short branches, 1-2 mm long, or essentially undivided with three apical stigmatic lobes. In other respects the species broadly resembles M. collina and particularly M. minor in the tepal claws forming a narrow cup including the stamens. In M. minor the style divides at or below the midline of the anthers, and the well-developed style branches are fairly broad and at least 3 mm long, bearing distinct crests. The ovary and capsules of M. longistyla are usually well-exserted from the spathes, while those of M. minor are typically enclosed, at least during development, although the ripe capsules are usually exserted. Moraea longistyla and M. minor have complementary distribution ranges, with M. minor always in sandy soils from the Cape Peninsula northward along the west coast into the Olifants River Valley.

claims.text: One of the so-called ‘peacock moraeas’, Moraea loubseri is readily recognised by the striking dark blue-violet flowers with the outer tepal claws and proximal parts of the limbs densely covered with dark blue-black hairs. The flowers are relatively large with outer tepals 24-30 x 12-18 mm. As in several other species of the M. villosa alliance, the solitary, linear leaf is velvety-hairy on the outer surface and the stem is minutely velvety. The inner tepals are 3-lobed with a particularly long, slender central lobe spreading to laxly reflexed and the style branches and crests are unusual in spreading horizontally rather than ascending as in other species of the M. villosa group.

claims.text: A fairly typical member of subg. Homeria, Moraea louisabolusiae has flowers with subequal tepals, all bearing nectar guides, short, erect tepal claws, and filaments largely united in a slender column but free in the distal 0.5-1.0 mm. The style branches are ± 2.5 mm long, shorter than the anthers, and bear short crests up to 1.5 mm long. Plants have a solitary, narrow foliage leaf inserted well above ground level and the stem is flexed outward above the sheathing part of the leaf. Apart from the single foliage leaf, the stem bears only sheathing leaves with attenuate apices. The flowers open early in the morning, at first light, and fade between 13:00 and 14:00. Molecular studies place M. louisabolusiae close to M. patens, which also has a solitary foliage leaf and the stem flexed above the leaf sheath but somewhat different flowers.

claims.text: Immediately recognised by the small, violet to pale blue flower with feathery or fringed style crests, unique in Moraea and reminiscent of the related genus Ferraria. The species also recalls Ferraria in the stigmatic surfaces located at the lateral tips of style branches. Both floral morphology and molecular phylogenetic studies place M. lugubris close to the base of phylogenetic trees, in some it is retrieved as sister to the remaining species of Moraea. The corm is of the Moraea type, thus consisting of a single internode with an apical bud and enclosed by well-developed tunics. The tunics of coarse fibres loosely enclosing the corm body are, however, unique in the genus.

claims.text: Variable in flower colour and to some extent in tepal shape, the perianth of Moraea lurida is typically an unusual dark liverish maroon and unpleasantly scented but is sometimes marked with yellow, through orange, violet, brown to creamy white. Both the dark and the lighter coloured flowers, the latter evidently unscented, seem equally attractive to muscid, dung and game flies that visit them in large numbers and are likely the legitimate pollinators. Also unusual in Moraea, the bases of the tepal claws lack discrete nectaries and nectar is secreted over the claw surface along vein lines. While the outer tepals are fairly uniform in shape, with the limbs shorter than the claws, the inner tepal limbs vary from fairly broad and entire to truly tricuspidate with a fairly long coiled central cusp and shorter, obtuse lateral lobes.

claims.text: Immediately recognised by its low stature, mostly 40-80 mm in height with stem underground or barely exserted at flowering, single narrow, falcate to trailing foliage leaf, and elongate, included ovary, 17-22 mm long. The capsules are even longer, up to 36 mm long and remain largely included in the spathes. Apart from the unusually long ovary, the flowers differ little from those of M. fugax and M. filicaulis and it has the beaked ovary of those two species. Capsules of M. filicaulis are usually 8-15 mm long and those of M. fugax typically 15-27 mm long vs 18-36 mm in M. macrocarpa. The tepals of M. macrocarpa are either blue-mauve, the outer with deep yellow nectar guides at the bases of the limbs edged in dark purple or in subsp. virginea white, also with yellow nectar guides, but lacking dark edges.

claims.text: Spring-flowering Moraea marionae is an inconspicuous plant and even in bloom the small, white to pale blue flowers are difficult to spot in the resprouting grass. As a result it remains poorly documented over its relatively wide range. The outer tepals are only 10-20 mm long, the limbs rarely longer than 12 mm, and the inner tepals are 3-lobed with small, rounded lateral lobes and a linear central cusp that is coiled inward. The terete leaf is often absent or just emergent at flowering time and attains its full length during the summer after the capsules have ripened. No plants with fully developed leaves are known. Its relationships are most likely with M. trifida, also of eastern southern Africa but with larger, brown to greenish flowers, also with 3-lobed inner tepals, but a channelled leaf present at flowering.

claims.text: With very small, white flowers, Moraea minima has nearly prostrate leaves with flat or shallowly channelled blades and style branches with entire stigmatic lobes. The flowers have a perianth tube only 7-10 mm long and tepals 9-12 mm long. Possibly most closely related to M. melanops or M. versicolor, both of which have larger, pink to purple flowers, M. minima differs significantly in having a short style so that the stigma lobes reach only to the middle of the anthers, the pollen thus in direct contact with the stigmas, and the species is self-compatible and, under greenhouse conditions, autogamous. The similarity of the small white flowers of M. minima to those of M. albiflora, which is also autogamous, is superficial and M. albiflora has the fringed style branches typical of ser. Galaxia. Moraea minima has a unique chromosome number in subg. Galaxia, a derived diploid number of 2n = 12, the lowest number in the genus.

claims.text: A diploid, self-compatible and autogamous species, Moraea minor has fugaceous flowers, opening in the late morning and fading in the middle of the afternoon of the same day. The flowers are similar to but slightly smaller that those of M. collina, having tepal claws forming narrow cup including the stamens and style branches, but the capsules are smaller, 25-28 mm long and without a beak, whereas the longer capsules of M. collina are typically 30-40 mm long, with an obtuse beak. On the Cape Peninsula, where both M. collina and M. minor occur, the species are separated by a difference in flowering times, although they may be sympatric and have similar soil preferences. Moraea minor flowers in late August and September there, while M. collina blooms from June onwards and is usually in seed by August. Moraea minor is closely allied to M. longistyla, which occurs east of the range of M. minor and usually on clay or rocky ground, and their differences are discussed under that species. Flowers of M. minor are fugaceous, whereas those of M. collina and M. longistyla last two or three days.

claims.text: Plants 500-700 mm high, always solitary. Corm 15-20 mm diam.; tunics of matted, brown fibres. Stem unbranched, covered by (2)3 or 4, green sheathing leaves, not usually overlapping, apices dry, brown. Foliage leaf linear, channelled, exceeding stem, trailing distally, mostly 11-15 mm wide. Rhipidial spathes green, with acute, dry tips, inner 9-16 mm long, inner slightly shorter. Flowers long-lived, yellow, creamy yellow or white, outer tepal limbs with bright yellow nectar guides at bases edged with a ring of purple veins; outer tepals broadly lanceolate, obtuse, 40-75 x 30-35 mm, claws ± 2/3 as long as limbs; inner tepals broadly lanceolate with tapering base, obtuse to retuse, up to 40-60 x 20-25 mm long, erect. Filaments ± 10 mm long, united in lower 1/2; anthers ± 10 mm long. Ovary cylindric, 20-30 mm long; style branches 18-20 mm long, crests 10-20 mm long, erect. Capsules cylindric-3-lobed, 30-40 mm long. Seeds flattened, disc-like.

claims.text: Distinguished in subg. Grandiflorae by its solitary habit, long, narrow, channelled leaf 11-15 mm wide, often with a grey blush, and very large, pale yellow to white flowers. The outer tepals are up to 75 mm long and the inner up to 60 mm long. It is most easily confused with M. spathulata, some forms of which are similar, but the two can usually be distinguished by the solitary habit of M. moggii compared with typically clump-forming M. spathulata, which has broader leaves often flat or very widely channelled and usually darker yellow flowers. Apart from this, M. moggii is generally a late flowering species, while M. spathulata flowers in spring or summer, except for some southern KwaZulu-Natal populations that also flower late in the season. Two subspecies are recognised, northern subsp. moggii, with pale yellow flowers, and southern subsp. albescens which typically has white or creamy yellow flowers.

claims.text: One of the smallest of the yellow-flowered species of subg. Grandiflorae, Moraea muddii stands 150-600 mm tall and is normally a solitary plant with soft, brown, irregularly broken cataphylls. The pale yellow flowers have tepals up to 50 mm long, thus of moderate size for the subgenus. Similar M. unibracteata is also of relatively low stature but has slightly smaller flowers and is easily distinguished by its single sheathing leaf inserted in the upper part of the stem, leaving the lower half visible vs. two or three overlapping sheathing leaves in M. muddii. Plants from Eastern Cape flowering somewhat later in the season and currently included in M. muddii probably represent a separate subspecies or even species but too little is known about them to permit an informed decision about their status. The leaves stand out in having a V-shaped keel instead of the rounded keel elsewhere in subg. Grandiflorae.

claims.text: Stands out in the solitary basal leaf with a long, narrowly channelled blade, straight margins and relatively large, blue or white flowers. Typical of sect. Deserticolae, the ovary is included in the spathes and as far as known, the capsules are beaked, a feature of some members of the M. saxicola complex. When described only white-flowered plants were known but the population from near Port Nolloth has blue-mauve flowers somewhat larger that those of those from Namibia, the outer tepals up to 47 mm long and the inner up to 40 mm long. Other features of the Port Nolloth population are similarly slightly larger that previously recorded, particularly the style crests, up to 25 mm long.

claims.text: Flowers of Moraea nana are of the Hexaglottis-type and closely resemble those of Moraea sect. Hexaglottis in their spreading, subequal tepals with short erect claws and style branches reduced to paired filiform arms, but the resemblance is convergent and M. nana has a vegetative form almost identical to that of some species of subg. Umbellatae, with leaves and branches crowded together above the ground. Chromosome number n = 10, also matches subg. Umbellatae (subg. Hexaglottis has x = 6). Moraea nana is probably most closely allied to M. maximiliani and the two can only be distinguished by examination of the floral parts: M. maximiliani has tepal claws ± 6 mm long, entirely united filaments, and short, apically diverging style branches partly hidden by the short erect and contiguous anthers, whereas M. nana has shorter tepal claws, 2-4 mm long, filaments free in the upper half, and filiform, spreading style branches extending between the filaments. Moraea nana and M. maximiliani are interfertile but neither can be crossed with species of sect. Hexaglottis. Flowers typically open after midday, ± 12:30 and collapse after 18:00 but in plants from the Pakhuis area of the northern Cederberg flowers open at ± 8:00 and deliquesce at ± 13:00. Flowers of these populations are slightly smaller than is typical but otherwise do not appear to differ significantly.

claims.text: With moderate-sized, blue-mauve to violet flowers, only the outer tepals with nectar guides, and well-developed style branches and crests, Moraea natalensis has unexceptional flowers for subg. Polyanthes but stands out in having a solitary foliage leaf inserted well above the ground on a stem with a long basal internode. The leaf is green at flowering and narrowly channelled, sometimes with the margins tightly inrolled and thus apparently terete. The few to several branches are short and somewhat crowded above the axil of the foliage leaf. This distinctive growth form is shared among the eastern southern African species of the subgenus only with M. inclinata, a taller plant, usually with darker violet flowers, green rhipidial spathes with the outer only about half as long as the inner, and nearly globose capsules. In M. natalensis the rhipidial spathes are often almost dry at flowering with the outer spathe only slightly shorter than the inner, and the capsules are obovoid to club-shaped.

claims.text: The large yellow or yellow and orange flowers of Moraea ochroleuca are distinctive in their wide cup formed by the tepal claws and spreading tepal limbs. The species is unusual in having nectar secreted from veins over the claw surface rather than from discrete nectaries at the tepal bases as in most other Moraea species. The style branches, relatively well developed and up to 6.5 mm long but only ± as wide as the anthers that are appressed to them, terminate in bilobed stigma lobes but lack discrete crests. The tall plants, up to 750 mm high, typically have a solitary foliage leaf but plants with two, or even three foliage leaves are known, these mostly from higher elevations. Flowers of M. ochroleuca last three days, opening in the morning on the first day and fading gradually during the third day. The flowers have a strong, rather sickly sweet, slightly fermenting odour.

claims.text: Plants 150-200(-380) mm high. Corm 6-12 mm diam.; tunics of hard, wiry, black fibres. Stem usually unbranched, 2 or 3 internodes long, sheathing leaves with dry attenuate tips, 30-45 mm long. Foliage leaf solitary, sometimes with second leaf from axillary cormlet, usually shorter than stem, rarely longer, 2-3 mm wide when opened flat, widely channelled or leaf halves almost folded together, inserted or shortly below ground level, usually bearing small axillary cormlet. Rhipidial spathes with dry, brown, attenuate tips, inner up to 55 mm long, outer ± 1/2 as long. Flowers long-lived, pale blue, outer tepal limbs with triangular yellow nectar guides at bases and dark veins radiating from nectar guides; outer tepals 27-29 mm long, claws 12-14 mm long, limbs ovate, ± 15 mm long, inner tepals hair-like, up to 4 mm long. Filaments ± 5 mm long, united ± 1 mm; anthers ± 6 mm long, dark blue-black; pollen white. Ovary linear-cylindric, 10-13 mm long, darkly lined vertically on locules and septa; style branches ± 12 mm long, crests ± linear, 8-12 mm long. Capsules ± cylindric, (15-)20-24 x 2 mm. Seeds angular, 0.8-1.5 mm diam., golden-brown, shortly winged on angles.

claims.text: A member of the Moraea tripetala complex of species, M. ogamana has hair-like inner tepals ± 4 mm long but is distinguished by the linear-cylindric ovary 10-13 mm long, often partly included in the spathes, and pale blue flowers with dark radiating venation and yellow nectar guides on the outer tepals. Associated with these features are the short stature, rarely exceeding 180 mm, fairly small corms, 7-12 mm diam., with wiry, black tunic fibres and a relatively short leaf, usually shorter than, but occasionally exceeding the stem. Unlike most populations of M. tripetala in the Western Cape forelands, which have orange-red pollen, the pollen of M. ogamana is white. An additional, but somewhat trivial distinction, the style crests, up to 12 mm, are unusually long for the relatively small flowers. Plants usually have a single small cormlet in the foliage leaf axil, and this modest level of vegetative reproduction results in plants sometimes growing in small clumps of three or four individuals. Correlated with the long, angular ovary, the capsules are ± cylindric and normally 20-24 mm long. Capsules of M. tripetala are ellipsoid-oblong and only 10-14 mm long. The seasonally waterlogged habitat is distinctive for M. ogamana.

claims.text: Plants up to 350 mm high. Corm 8-11 mm diam.; tunics brown, ± woody, inner layers entire, outer splitting from base. Stem mostly 3 or 4(5) internodes long, with 1 or 2 branches at each node, branches slightly flexed above sheath of subtending leaf. Leaves 3 to 5, lowermost longest, inserted 10-20 mm above ground, linear, channelled, ± straight or loosely twisted, up to 450 mm long, upper leaves progressively shorter, none entirely sheathing. Rhipidial spathes: inner 35-40 mm long, ± truncate, apex brown, somewhat lacerated, outer 1/2-2/3 as long, with acute, brown apex. Flowers buff-yellow, lightly brown-veined, outer tepals darkly veined abaxially, limbs with deep yellow nectar guides at bases edged brown, spreading slightly below horizontal, inner tepals with reddish brown spot at bases of limbs, similarly spreading, outer tepals 30-32 mm long, limbs 20-22 x 10-12 mm, claws ± 10 mm long, inner tepals oblanceolate, ± 22 x 5-6 mm. Filaments 8-9 mm long, united in lower 5-6 mm, diverging distally; anthers dark purple, 3.5-5.0 mm long; pollen red. Ovary exserted, oblong-elliptic, 5-6 mm long; style branches ± 10 mm long, crests 10-14 mm long, erect, narrowly wedge-shaped. Capsules narrowly obovoid, 9-11 mm long. Seeds softly angular, ± 1 mm long, with rugulo-reticulate surface, light yellow-brown.

claims.text: One of few species of subg. Umbellatae with leaves basal and cauline rather than crowded at the first aerial node, Moraea orthrosantha has a flower typical of the genus, with well-developed style branches and crests and nectar guides only on the outer tepals. The flowers are dull yellow with conspicuous dark veins and closely resemble those of M. margaretae. As the specific epithet suggests, flowers open soon after sunrise and collapse about noon (Greek, orthros = morning, anthos = flower). The flowers of most species of subg. Umbellatae open in the mid- to late morning and wilt and collapse in the late afternoon, and only a few other examples of morning flowering phenology are known in Moraea, notably in M. vlokii and three Namaqualand species of subg. Homeria, M. flexicaulis, M. knersvlaktensis and M. schlechteri. Records for M. margaretae, with which M. orthrosantha is most easily confused, indicate flowers open midmorning and collapse toward sunset.

claims.text: Despite its several synonyms, Moraea pallida is relatively uniform both in the small yellow flowers and low stature with a solitary leaf clasping the lower half of the stem. The flowers have spreading tepal limbs 16-24 mm long and erect claws, ± 3 mm long, clasping the lower part of the filament column. Somewhat unusually for the genus, the filaments are free and diverging distally for 1-2 mm, a feature shared with M. cookii to which it appears to be closely related. The relatively short style branches reach only to the middle of the anthers but have short crests, either erect or curving inward. Populations from KwaZulu-Natal differ somewhat in having numerous small cormlets around the base of the parent corm and even in the axils of the foliage and sheathing leaves. Plants bloom in spring to early summer usually at the end of the dry winter, before the onset of the summer-rainfall season.

claims.text: With a relatively open flower, Moraea patens has tepal claws inclined gently upward forming a wide, shallow cup that includes the filament column and with the tepal limbs extending laxly outward. claims.text: Flowering in the dry season, the solitary, long, trailing leaf up to 1 m long is dry or almost so when flowering begins. The relatively small, blue flowers are distinctive, resembling those of sect. Hexaglottis in having subequal tepals with short erect claws, free stamens, and style branches divided to the base into filiform arms extending between the stamens. Plastid DNA data confirm an alliance with Moraea crispa and M. pseudospicata, both of which have small, blue flowers with partly united filaments and flattened style branches forked at the tips and appressed to the subtending anthers. The leaf of M. pearsonii is linear and narrowly channelled when fresh, but with the margins tightly inrolled on drying so that the leaf then appears to be terete. The main stem and branches bear sessile rhipidia at the upper nodes, a pattern found in several species of the section, including M. pseudospicata and M. verecunda, both Western Karoo endemics.

claims.text: One of the tallest species of subg. Homeria, standing up to 750 mm, Moraea pendula has several, glaucous-grey foliage leaves and bright yellow, nodding to completely pendent flowers that are unusual in having the tepal limbs tightly reflexed against the pedicels. The filaments are fully united in a column abruptly swollen above the base and tapering to a narrow apex, and the tepal claws, ± 4 mm long, clasp the bulbous part of the filament column. Typically the anthers and pollen are orange-red and provide a contrast to the yellow tepals. Moraea pendula is evidently closely related to the widespread M. miniata, which has smaller, spreading tepals but a similar filament column swollen at the base. Both occur in the Kamiesberg but M. pendula blooms later in the year and grows in wetter sites than M. miniata.

claims.text: Plants ± 30 mm high. Corm globose, ± 12-16 mm diam.; tunics of grey-brown, medium-textured, netted fibres, accumulating in fibrous collar around base of stem. Stem with 3 aerial internodes, unbranched, sheathing leaves with dry attenuate apices, 35-40 mm long. Foliage leaf solitary, basal, linear, narrowly channelled, 2/3 to ± as long as stem, ± 2 mm wide opened flat. Rhipidial spathes with dry, attenuate apices, inner ± 40 mm long, outer ± half as long. Flowers lasting 3 days, purple, outer tepal limbs with white, wedge-shaped nectar guides at bases, laxly spreading to weakly reflexed; outer tepals ± 20 mm long, claws ± 6 mm long, ascending; inner tepals ± 9 mm long, limbs spreading, ± 4 mm long, 3-lobed with long, tapering central cusp and short, rounded, obtuse lateral lobes, claws ± 5 mm long, ascending, tapering from narrow base to wide apex. Filaments ± 8 mm long, united in smooth cylindric column in lower ± 3 mm, diverging in upper 5 mm; anthers ± 5 mm long, dark purple; pollen red. Ovary ± cylindric, ± 8 mm long, exserted; style branches ± 8 x 2 mm long, ascending, held above subtending limbs, crests narrowly wedge-shaped, ± 4 mm long. Capsules and seeds unknown.

claims.text: A typical member of subg. Vieusseuxia in its solitary basal leaf and 3-lobed inner tepals. The purple flowers are assumed to be long-lasting and the outer tepal limbs have narrow, white, wedge-shaped nectar guides edged with dark purple. The inner tepals have unusually broad, 3-lobed limbs with a prominent, linear, reflexed central cusp and rounded lateral lobes. The flowers in general recall M. decipiens, particularly in the flower colour and shape but have much longer filaments, ± 8 mm long vs. 3.5-4.0 mm in M. decipiens, a style ± 5 mm long (vs. ± 2 mm) and shorter tepal claws, 5-6 mm (vs. 8-9 mm). The relatively long style branches are held well above the subtending outer tepals limbs, whereas in M. decipiens the style branches are appressed to the tepal claws and the inner tepals curve upward rather than having reflexed limbs with the central cusp directed downward. Additional collections of this rare species are needed to confirm current observations based on limited material.

claims.text: A relatively small plant, Moraea pilifolia has pale yellow flowers with a perianth tube up to 10 mm long and tepals 6-10 mm long, otherwise typical of ser. It most closely resembles M. galaxia, which has broader, usually prostrate leaves, the margins with short cilia, and larger flowers with tepals 16-20 mm long.

claims.text: Plants 150-350 mm high. Corm obconic-subglobose, 25-40 mm diam., bearing numerous small cormlets at base; tunics brown, outer layers becoming fibrous, with strong vertical ribs joined by fine fibres. Stem sticky below nodes, usually branching at all nodes, with 2, rarely 3, branches per node, with cauline sheathing leaves up to 28 mm long, dry and brown in distal 5-6 mm, ± truncate or subacute. Foliage leaves 2, lowermost up to 40 x 4-6 mm (opened flat), inserted below ground, linear, channelled, longest, initially suberect, trailing above, upper leaf somewhat shorter. Rhipidial spathes subacute to ± truncate, purple near tips, aging dry and brown, inner 22-25 mm long, outer 1/2-2/3 as long. Flowers fugaceous, slate blue-grey to purple, outer tepals coppery pink outside and limbs with off white nectar guides minutely speckled with blue dots at bases, claws whitish, minutely speckled grey-blue; outer tepals ± 18 x 5.5-7.0 mm, initially spreading, later half reflexed often recurving distally, claws ± 10 mm long, thus slightly exceeding limbs, suberect; inner tepals up to 14 x 3 mm, oblanceolate, limbs spreading horizontally or later half reflexed. Filaments ± 8 mm long, free but closely cohering in smooth, cylindric column ± 6.5 mm long, diverging near apex; anthers 3-4 mm long, dark purple; pollen orange-red. Ovary ± 8 mm long, usually included; style branches ± 6 x 2 mm, sharply diverging and extended horizontally, white, flushed purple distally; stigma lobe transverse, with prominent stigmatic appendage ± 2 mm long, acute or apex forked, crests arching upward, 4-5 mm long, purple. Capsules and seeds unknown.

claims.text: Moraea saldanhensis has relatively small, slate-blue flowers, the outer tepals ± 18 mm long with spreading and ultimately half reflexed limbs ± 8 mm long thus shorter than the claws ± 10 mm long. It is most easily confused with M. inconspicua which has similarly small flowers (outer tepals 12-18 mm long), usually yellow to brown, occasionally white to cream-coloured, but the tepal limbs are almost always fully reflexed and somewhat to twice as long as the upright claws. Moraea saldanhensis also has a slightly longer filament column, ± 6.5 mm long (vs 3.5-6.0 mm in southern populations of M. inconspicua), orange-red pollen and the ovary is included whereas in M. inconspicua the ovary is usually exserted and the pollen is typically yellow, although populations with red pollen are known, notably among the Namaqualand populations, segregated as subsp. namaquensis.

claims.text: Late-flowering Moraea saxicola is recognised by the solitary foliage leaf with thickened, straight to undulate margins, and relatively large flowers with outer tepals 34-45 mm long and the limbs of both whorls half reflexed. The tepals are usually pale blue in the north of its range, white to palest yellow elsewhere, and the outer tepal limbs bear pale yellow nectar guides. The foliage leaf is fairly broad and slightly undulate with occasionally slightly crisped margins. Unusual for Moraea, the juvenile leaves are narrow and sometimes terete and coiled near the apex. By the time these plants reach flowering age, the leaf is usually broad, channelled and trailing. Moraea saxicola is allied to the yellow-flowered M. bolusii of northern Namaqualand, which also has an undulate leaf.

claims.text: Evidently one of the least specialised species of subg. Homeria, Moraea schlechteri has several foliage leaves, the lower longest, but even those on the upper nodes normally have expanded blades. The flowers are pale yellow and have small darker yellow nectar guides on all tepals, these with short, poorly differentiated claws ± 1 mm long. The filaments are united in a slender column but are free in the upper 0.5-1.0 mm, and the well-developed style branches are slightly wider than the anthers and have prominent crests 2 mm long. Closely related M. knersvlaktensis has a similar vegetative form, though with broader, undulate leaves, the lowermost inserted well above the ground and even the outer rhipidial spathes are somewhat leafy, sheathing the inner spathes only in the lower half. The flowers of the two species are structurally nearly identical but the nectar guides are more prominent in M. knersvlaktensis, the tepals claws 2 mm long, and the filament column sparsely and shortly hairy. Both M. schlechteri and M. knersvlaktensis have morning flowers that fade soon after midday.

claims.text: A small plant, Moraea serpentina rarely attains 200 mm in height and 90-120 mm is usual. It is readily distinguished by the typically three, rarely two or four foliage leaves, the blades channelled or flat and always at least loosely twisted, sometimes tightly so. The flowers are either partly yellow with pale yellow or white style branches and crests or white with the inner tepals and style branches flushed with violet. The inner tepals are held erect, a striking feature of the species. In the Kamiesberg populations the leaves are hairy on the margins or abaxial surface. Closely related M. tortilis, restricted to northern Namaqualand, has a broadly similar appearance but the leaf blades are terete and tightly coiled in corkscrew fashion, and the violet or white flowers have both outer and inner tepal limbs invariably half reflexed. Populations of Moraea serpentina from the western Knersvlakte, north of Vredendal, stand out in having consistently smaller, pale blue-violet flowers and two or even a single leaf but evidently do not otherwise differ from white-flowered plants. One- or two-leaved plants are occasionally found elsewhere across its range.

claims.text: Readily distinguished in sect. Gynandriris by its low stature and small flowers. The blue-mauve flowers have orange and white nectar guides on the outer tepals, 12-18 mm long, and the limbs of both outer and inner tepals are half reflexed. The small flower size is reflected in the short filaments 3.5-6.0 mm long and short anthers up to 4 mm long. The flowers open between noon and 13:00 and fade shortly before sunset. Several populations examined for chromosome number are diploid, 2n = 12, and plants have been found in the greenhouse to be reproductively self-compatible and autogamous. They thus produce ample seed wherever they occur. This mode of reproduction is unusual in Moraea but explains its success as a weed.

claims.text: Living plants of Moraea simulans are readily recognised by their distinctive flowers with the tepals speckled throughout with darker mauve to violet blotches on a pale blue-lilac background, a feature unique in the section but unfortunately not visible when dry. The flowers are moderate in size, having outer tepals 17-28 mm long and both inner and outer tepals are rather narrow with laxly spreading to half reflexed limbs. Flowers open in the middle of the afternoon, usually after 15:30 and last just a few hours, collapsing after 19:00. Despite its several synonyms, M. simulans is not particularly variable except in height and the number of branches, features dependent on growing conditions rather than genetically determined. The species is evidently polyploid but chromosome numbers are known from only two collections, one tetraploid, 2n = 24, and the other hexaploid, 2n = 36.

claims.text: Plant small, acaulescent 30-40 mm high. Corm spindle-shaped, ± 10 mm diam., tunics of grey-brown, wiry, reticulate fibres. Stem with 1 to 4 sessile branches clustered at ground level. Leaves 3, clustered at ground level, lowermost longest, inserted on stem at ground level, falcate, terete, 50-80 mm long, 0.8-1.0 mm diam., upper 2 leaves much shorter, recurved, bifacial, channelled or with short terete blade up to 20 mm long. Rhipidial spathes green, 25-30 mm long, outer leaf-like, spreading distally, ± as long as inner. Flowers rotate, pale to golden-yellow, limbs of all tepals with brown, spear- or lozenge-shaped nectar guide near bases, tepal claws ascending, forming a cup enclosing base of filament column, limbs spreading, inner usually twisted through 90º distally; tepals united for 2 mm, claws ± 1 mm long, limbs obovate-pandurate, truncate, outer ± 12 x 6 mm, inner slightly smaller. Filaments ± 5 mm long, connate in a smooth, cylindric column ± 4 mm long, free and diverging in upper 1 mm; anthers ± 3 mm long, arched, yellow; pollen yellow. Ovary cylindric, ± 10 mm long, included; style branches divided almost to base into paired terete arms extending either side of each anther, ± 1.5 mm long, stigmatic at apices, crests reduced, ± 1 mm long. Capsules and seeds unknown.

claims.text: An acaulescent species, Moraea singularis also stands out in the short, terete leaf blades. The yellow flowers, with both inner and outer tepals limbs bearing brown nectar guides, have tepal claws only ± 1 mm long that form a narrow cup including the base of the smooth filament column. The tepal limbs are oblanceolate-pandurate, the inner three slightly smaller than the outer and twisted through 90º. The asymmetric corms with brown corm tunics accord best with subg. Umbellatae, as do the outer rhipidial spathes, which sheath the inner only in the lower half and arch outward distally, and also the yellow flowers with darkly veined tepals and brown nectar guides. Unique to the subgenus is the terete blade of the basal leaf, while the upper leaves are channelled entirely or for part of their length and terete distally.

claims.text: Somewhat variable across its wide range, Moraea spathulata typically forms large tufts, thus it is not unusual to see several flowers open at once. Each flowering stem bears a single broad leaf, shallowly channelled to almost flat. The species can be distinguished by its large yellow flowers, the outer tepals up to 50 mm long, tall stems, and clump-forming habit. Plants flower in late winter and spring along the coast but in summer and autumn inland. The species comprises numerous local races, but owing to the small differences between them, it is difficult to define many of them. Four subspecies were described in Goldblatt (1973) but are not currently recognised.

claims.text: The wet habitat is distinctive for Moraea stagnalis, which has flowers almost identical with those of other members of ser. Galaxia but with the filaments usually free in the upper third. The style divides opposite the anthers and the stigmatic fringes of the style branches are always in contact with the anthers and pollen. The narrow, shallowly channelled leaves have smooth to minutely ciliate margins. Moraea stagnalis is polyploid, 2n = 36, and in the laboratory is autogamous. The species is most easily confused with M. fugacissima, which has larger flowers with a perianth tube mostly 15-24 mm long, anthers up to 4 mm long, and the style usually exceeding the anthers rather than tangled among them. The filaments of M. fugacissima are usually completely united whereas those of M. stagnalis are typically, though not invariably, free in the upper third.

claims.text: Recognised by the combination of a dry (or absent) foliage leaf at flowering, a fairly short stem up to 250 mm high, and small, pale blue-mauve to lilac flowers. Only the outer tepals bear nectar guides and the style branches are relatively well developed and bear short, erect crests ± 3 mm long. The foliage leaf, also distinctive, is emergent at or soon after flowering, and has a terete, prominently ribbed blade with a thickened apex. Ultimately the leaf may be up to 600 mm long or longer, then trailing through low, grassy vegetation. At the end of the growing season the leaf turns dry and brown and the flowering stem to which it is attached begins to elongate in preparation for flowering the following spring. Flowering at the end of the dry season, the rhipidial spathes and sheathing leaves are, like the foliage leaf, usually dry and brown. Moraea stricta is one of relatively few polyploid species.

claims.text: Closely related to Moraea deserticola from the Knersvlakte, M. tanquana is distinguished by the three linear foliage leaves up to 5 mm wide, pale blue to mauve flowers with subequal tepals ± 22 mm long, united filaments, and short, contiguous anthers, 4-5 mm long that exceed the style branches and enclose them. The style divides opposite the lower third of the anthers so that the stigmatic tips of the short style branches, ± 1 mm long, emerge from between the middle of the ± contiguous anthers, and the branches lack crests. A smaller plant, M. deserticola has narrow foliage leaves 2-3 mm wide, tepals 30-36 mm long, and anthers 6.0-6.5 mm long (shrinking after anthesis to 5 mm) that remain contiguous around the style with their bases held within the floral cup. The ovary is conspicuously veined with dark red in M. deserticola but uniformly green in M. tanquana.

claims.text: Plants up to 200 mm high. Corm globose, 15-20 mm diam.; tunics forming dense, fibrous mass, dark grey-black. Stem simple or 1-branched, 3 internodes long, bearing sheathing leaves ± 25 mm long. Foliage leaves 2, basal, ± linear, evidently narrowly channelled, straight, possibly ± trailing distally, ± as long as stem, slightly < 1 mm diam. margins plane. Rhipidial spathes with broad, dry, transparent margins, inner ± 25 mm long, outer ± 1/2 as long. Flowers fugaceous, white with style branches flushed pale mauve, outer tepal limbs with large pale yellow nectar guides at bases white in middle, inner tepal claws speckled yellow, scent unknown; outer tepals ± 18 x 8 mm, claws ascending, ± 8 mm long, inner tepals ± 15 x 6 mm. Filaments ± 8 mm long, united below in smooth, cylindric column ± 4 mm long; anthers ± 4.5 mm long, pale mauve; pollen white. Ovary spindle-shaped, ± 7 mm long, included; style branches diverging, ± 6 mm long, crests broadly wedge-shaped, ± 7 mm long. Capsules ellipsoid, 9-10 mm long, without beak. Seeds unknown.

claims.text: Superficially a small-flowered morph of Moraea saxicola, M. teretifolia stands out in having two basal foliage leaves with straight, terete blades ± as long as the stem. Both closely related M. geminifolia and M. saxicola also have branched stems but larger flowers, the outer tepals of M. geminifolia 25-30 x 10 mm and those of M. saxicola 34-45 x 10-16 mm, whereas in M. teretifolia the outer tepals are ± 18 x 8 mm. The white flowers have large nectar guides at the base of the outer tepal limbs, the nectar guides with a white centre bracketed by broad yellow borders. The capsules of M. teretifolia are 9-10 mm long and differ from those of M. saxicola in lacking a beak. Capsules of M. saxicola are 12-14 mm long with short beak up to 1 mm long.

claims.text: Superficially like Moraea angusta (subg. Monocephalae) in its pale yellow flowers with lanceolate, entire inner tepals, stamens united only near the base, and unbranched stem, M. thomasiae otherwise has a single channelled leaf inserted near the stem base and long-lasting flowers. These two features, as well as the chromosome number, 2n = 12, accord best with subg. Vieusseuxia and molecular phylogenetic studies also place M. thomasiae among the species of this subgenus but without close relatives. Most other species of the subg. Vieusseuxia have reduced inner tepals, most often with 3-lobed limbs, sometimes a linear cusp, or even lacking.

claims.text: Recognised by its broadly triangular style crests 8-10 x 5 mm and relatively short style branches, up to 5 mm long, ± half as long as the crests. In the Atlantic Coast forelands of Western Cape flowers are either predominantly deep pink to brick-red (flower colour in the type of the species) or yellow or, in the Saldanha area, violet, and have virtually hairless leaves and spathes. In the Caledon District plants grow in renosterveld on clay ground and have pale purple flowers, and the leaves and spathes are velvet. Added to these differences is a difference in chromosome number, 2n = 18 in the west but 20 in the Caledon District. Populations further east in the De Hoop area and near Still Bay have yellow flowers and resemble the western populations morphologically but bloom earlier in the year, in May and June versus July to September in the west.

claims.text: Readily distinguished in sect. Vieusseuxia by the comparatively large, white or sometimes pale creamy yellow flowers with spreading, comparatively broad tepal limbs forming a wide cup. The inner tepal limbs are 3-lobed with rounded lateral lobes and a slender central lobe up to 5 mm long, usually obliquely coiled inward (sometimes straight in subsp. parviflora). Closely allied to M. bellendenii and sometimes barely distinguishable from it without knowledge of flower colour, M. tricuspidata is a shorter plant, rarely exceeding 500 mm in height, whereas M. bellendenii has deep yellow flowers and is a taller, more slender species, 500-1000 mm high. Slight but apparently consistent differences in size of floral parts can usually be relied upon to distinguish them. Although they have somewhat different habitat preferences and flowering times, the two occasionally grow close to one another at sites on the Cape Peninsula, where hybrids between the two occur, these intermediate in height and with pale yellow flowers.

claims.text: One of several eastern southern African species of sect. The outer tepal limbs are broadly ovate, longer than wide and oriented ± 45° below horizontal. The corm tunics are dark brown to grey and usually composed of medium-textured fibres. The production of cormlets is not known in M. tripetala. Nectar guides are often yellow edged with dark blue or purple, but occasionally white, then dotted with blue to purple. The seeds are small, and typical of the complex in being 5(6)-sided with the facets slightly wrinkled and showing the brown colour of the seed body. The angles are raised into narrow wings of paler colour. Related species including M. amabilis, M. cuspidata and M. grandis have larger seeds of more complex structure.

claims.text: Resembling Moraea villosa in its velvety stems and outer leaf surfaces, M. tulbaghensis typically has bright orange flowers with navy blue to glossy, emerald green nectar guides. The flowers are usually somewhat smaller than those of M. villosa, the outer tepals 22-40 mm long, but the species is most easily distinguished by the anthers, 7-10 mm long and exceeding the style branches and often overtopping the particularly short crests ± 2 mm long. Western populations, recognised as Iris pavonia and later named M. neopavonia, sometimes have small, elliptic to obscurely three-lobed rather than the strongly tricuspidate inner tepals that characterise other populations, and are diploid, whereas the species is tetraploid elsewhere. Tepal markings in these populations are either navy blue or consist of small dark spots. Populations from Voëlvlei and at Elandsberg Nature Reserve have dark red rather than the more common orange flowers. Even more unusual, a white-flowered population occurs on the slopes of Kasteelberg.

claims.text: Moraea umbellata has the vegetative morphology typical of subg. Umbellatae, viz. a stem comprising a long basal internode, leaves clustered well above ground at the first aerial node where branching occurs, and several subequal branches clustered in semi-umbellate manner. Plants can be robust, reaching as much as 450 mm in height and can often be distinguished by size alone. The flowers are also distinctive with the tepal claws 5-7 mm long and enclosing the filaments, which are either united entirely or free near the apex, and reduced and narrow style branches appressed to but shorter than the anthers and lacking crests. The outer inflorescence spathes may be entirely sheathing or free distally as in several other species of the subgenus. The fugaceous flowers last only a few hours, opening in the late afternoon, fading in early evening and completely collapsed by 19:00. Individuals of three of four populations so far examined cytologically are triploid, 2n = 30, hence sexually sterile, and only one diploid population is known, 2n = 20. It seems likely that many populations of the species are triploid as plants often fail to set seed, and most collections lack developing capsules. Reproduction in the sexually sterile plants is evidently by the numerous tiny cormlets produced around the base of the mother corm.

claims.text: A slender plant with one of the smallest flowers in subg. Vieusseuxia, the outer tepals typically 12-18 mm long with limbs ± 8-10 mm long. Flowers are unusually varied in tepal orientation and colour. The most common morph has outer tepal limbs half reflexed and white to creamy yellow, darkly speckled near the base, but populations in the Ceres area of the Western Cape have attractive dark blue-violet tepals. A second morph, corresponding to the synonym, M. tenuis, has the outer tepal limbs fully reflexed and the tepals dull pinkish brown with pale yellow, velvety nectar guides. These morphs may represent separate taxa but so far attempts to refer all herbarium collections to one or other morph have failed owing to the presence of apparent intermediates. Plants consistently have filaments united in a slender, smooth column with only their tips free, comparatively narrow style branches, short narrow crests, and 3-lobed inner tepal limbs, the longer central lobe linear and symmetrically coiled inward. Evidently closely related, M. bellendenii and M. tricuspidata have larger flowers, also with 3-lobed inner tepals but with the central lobe asymmetrically coiled. Also easily confused with M. unguiculata, M. rivulicola has somewhat larger flowers of very similar structure but with outer tepals up to 24 mm long, unbearded tepal claws, and a larger ovary and capsule, the latter 25-32 mm long vs. 13-15 mm in M. unguiculata. The two species co-occur at some sites in Namaqualand in slightly different habitats. An odd variant of Moraea unguiculata from the Kamiesberg of central Namaqualand has linear, filiform inner tepals but otherwise seems to conform to the species. Typical M. unguiculata with 3-lobed inner tepals also occurs in the Kamiesberg.

claims.text: Plants up to 350 mm high, solitary. Corm ± 10 mm diam.; tunics of fine, pale fibres. Stem sheathed below by brown cataphylls, unbranched, bearing a single, green sheathing leaf inserted in upper part of stem, often overlapping rhipidial spathes, lower part of stem exposed. Foliage leaf solitary, shortly exceeding stem, channelled, (2-)4-10 mm wide. Rhipidial spathes green, apices dry and brown, inner spathe 60-80 mm long, outer ± 3/4 as long. Flowers ?long-lived, pale yellow to nearly white (sometimes drying pale blue), when dry veined with purple, outer tepal limbs with darker yellow nectar guides at bases, spreading to half reflexed; outer tepals lanceolate, 30-45 mm long, claws suberect, ± 2/3 as long as limbs; inner tepals 30-40 mm long, narrowly lanceolate, ± erect. Filaments ± 8 mm long, united in lower half; anthers 7-9 mm long, yellow. Ovary 15-18 mm long; style branches ± 10 mm long, crests 10-13 mm long. Capsules and seeds unknown.

claims.text: Poorly known, Moraea unibracteata is one of the smallest members of subg. Grandiflorae. It can always be recognised by the stem bearing a single sheathing leaf, this inserted in the upper half of the stem and usually reaching or overlapping the rhipidial spathes. The pale yellow to almost white flowers are unremarkable in the subgenus, although relatively small, with outer tepals 30-45 mm long and anthers 7-9 mm long. The tepals are reported to have dark veins, especially evident when dry.

claims.text: Although evidently a member of subg. Monocephalae, Moraea vallisavium has some unusual features for the alliance, particularly the finely fibrous corm tunics, the persistent old corms that accumulate beneath the current corm, and the leaf blade compressed and unifacial rather than terete. Also unusual, the margins of the sheathing leaf and outer rhipidial spathes are free to the base, whereas those of other species of the subgenus are united basally for a short distance. Like other members of the subgenus M. vallisavium has a solitary foliage leaf, an unbranched stem and fairly large yellow flowers. The seeds are unusual for subg. Monocephalae in their relatively large size ± angular shape, quite unlike the flattened discoid seeds of other species of the subgenus.

claims.text: Recognised by the solitary foliage leaf inserted on the stem well above ground, main stem and branches flexed above the sheaths of foliage or sheathing leaves, and a pink or yellow flower with the tepal claws diverging to form a relatively wide cup that includes the filaments. The filaments are united in a narrow column that is velvety in the lower half, and the diverging anthers slightly exceed the style branches, the crests of which are vestigial. It is apparently related to the more widespread M. minor of the Western Cape Atlantic Coast and Olifants River Valley and the two are easily confused, especially when dried. However, in M. minor the tepal claws form a narrow cup including both filaments and anthers and the short style branches have larger, clearly visible crests. Both species are diploid but M. minor is autogamous and M. vallisbelli is self-incompatible.

claims.text: With a reddish purple flower with yellow cup, Moraea variabilis most resembles M. versicolor but differs in the glossy, dark green leaves, channelled with straight margins, filaments usually united entirely or rarely free for less than 1 mm, thus with the anthers sessile or almost so, and the style dividing just above the anther tips. Moraea versicolor has the leaves usually glaucous and with wavy margins, the filaments free and diverging in the upper 1.0-1.5 mm, and the style dividing 2-3 mm above the tips of the anthers. The ranges of the two species are complimentary. Apparent hybrids with Moraea citrina have been recorded at a few sites and have large orange or pink flowers. The variation in flower size and colour among the hybrids suggests that they are interbreeding.

claims.text: Moraea vegeta with its several characteristic glaucous leaves, velvety stem, and somewhat pendulous capsules is not easily confused with related species with similar flowers such as M. papilionacea and M. gawleri (the latter its closest relative according to molecular data). Moraea indecora, restricted to northern Namaqualand, has similar drooping capsules but rather different habit and flowers, and may be immediately related but molecular evidence on the question is lacking. Moraea vegeta is one of the few species of the genus that has adapted to human settlement and it is most common, almost weedy, in parts of the Constantia area of the Cape Peninsula where it thrives under the naturalised oaks and pines. Moraea vegeta is also one of few species of Moraea that is self-compatible and autogamous in the absence of insect-mediated pollen transfer. The dull-coloured and inconspicuous flowers are consistent with this mode of reproduction.

claims.text: Plants medium to large, 200-300 mm high. Corm globose, 20-35 mm diam.; tunics of hard, dark medium-textured to coarse fibres. Stem several-branched, with green to partly to completely dry, attenuate sheathing leaves at upper nodes 30-50 mm long. Foliage leaves 3 to 6, lanceolate to linear, channelled to ± flat, as long or longer than stem, falcate, usually trailing distally, 8-30 mm wide, margins often thickened, hyaline. Rhipidial spathes green or turning brown and dry above, long attenuate, with broad, translucent margins, inner mostly 40-60 mm long, outer almost as long, margins free nearly to base. Flowers fugaceous, blue-violet, outer tepal limbs with yellow to orange nectar guides at bases, reflexed up to ± 40º; outer tepals mostly 45-60 x 18-25 mm, claws ± 22 mm long, inner 35-50 x 9-12 mm, evidently ± erect. Filaments 10-15 mm long, united in lower 2/3; anthers 8-9 mm long. Ovary ± cylindric, mostly 15-20 mm long, sometimes veined red, usually included; style branches ± 12 mm long, crests up to 15 mm long. Capsules narrowly obovoid, 16-20 mm long, nodding when mature. Seeds angular, ± 2 mm long.

claims.text: Moraea venenata has the several leaves, a branched stem, and blue-violet flowers much like those of M. polystachya, but is a more robust species, although often not as tall. The flowers have outer tepals 40-60 mm long with the claws 22-30 mm long, and as far as known the inner tepals are erect. The widest of the several leaves are up to 30 mm wide near the middle [vs. 6-12(-20) mm in M. polystachya] and the outer spathes are up to 60 mm long and the inner about half as long but with unusually broad, translucent margins, free almost to the base, an unusual feature among the southern African members of the genus.

claims.text: Moraea versicolor has pink to purple flowers with tepals forming a cup in the lower half, usually with a yellow centre but populations with a blue to violet centre occur locally. The leaves are usually somewhat glaucous and widely channelled and often somewhat twisted, with undulate margins. The filaments are free and diverging in the upper 1.0-1.5 mm and united in the lower part, usually forming a bottle-shaped column wider in the lower half but populations with a cylindric filament column occur in the Breede River Valley. The style divides above the anthers, often exceeding them by 3-4 mm. Moraea variabilis has similarly coloured flowers but glossy, channelled leaves with straight margins, and filaments united entirely or rarely free distally for less than 1 mm, with the style dividing just above the anther tips. The species is variable for chromosome number and most populations have a diploid number of 2n = 16 but plants from the northern Cape Peninsula and from the Tulbagh Valley have 2n = 14.

claims.text: Evidently closely related to the widespread M. brevistyla but the two are readily distinguished when alive. They grow within a few metres of one another on the slopes of The Sentinel where M. brevistyla grows on deeper soils on grassy slopes and M. vigilans is confined to basalt outcrops. The most striking difference between them is the broadly ovate to orbicular outer tepal limbs of M. vigilans, spreading or ascending up to 30°, whereas the narrower, oblanceolate-obovate outer tepal limbs of M. brevistyla are weakly to strongly reflexed and the limbs are usually pinched downward in the proximal third. Less apparent are the shorter outer tepal claws of M. vigilans, 7-9 mm long, and shorter filament column and style branches, the latter reaching opposite the apex of the outer tepal limb. The short, brownish crests extend upward above the base of the tepal limbs for up to 4 mm. The outer tepal claws of M. brevistyla are 9-11 mm long, the filaments and anthers are longer than those of M. vigilans (11-12 mm combined length in M. brevistyla vs. ± 8.5 mm in M. vigilans), and the style branches usually exceed the outer tepal limbs by up to 3.5 mm, while the white style crests extend upward a further 5 mm. Vegetatively the two species appear virtually identical but the stems of M. vigilans are somewhat willowy and incline toward the ground, whereas the stems of M. brevistyla are usually stiffly erect.

claims.text: Plants 450-700 mm high, solitary, rarely in small clumps, possibly evergreen. Corm up to 20 mm diam.; tunics of medium-textured fibres. Stem sheathed below by pale fibrous cataphyll up to 200 mm long forming a basket-like network, unbranched (rarely with a sessile lateral rhipidium), covered by 3 or 4 overlapping sheathing leaves, 120-150 mm long, green or becoming dry distally. Foliage leaf solitary, linear, channelled to ± flat, much exceeding stem, 12-15 mm wide, suberect, later trailing distally. Rhipidial spathes green with dry brown tips, inner 120-150 mm long, outer slightly shorter. Flowers long-lived, bright yellow, outer tepal limbs with large, orange nectar guides at bases, reflexed to ± 45º; outer tepals 65-70 x 25 mm; inner tepals 50-60 x 15 mm, ± erect. Filaments ± 13 mm long, united in lower 1/2; anthers ± 15 mm long, white; pollen white. Ovary cylindric, 20-30 mm long; style branches ± 20 mm long, crests 15-18 mm long. Capsules cylindric-3-lobed, 30-40 mm long. Seeds flattened, discoid.

claims.text: Allied to the widespread Moraea spathulata, the flowers of M. reticulata are almost identical in size and general aspect but the plants themselves differ in being almost invariably solitary. Moraea spathulata occurs in the same areas as M. reticulata but blooms from November to January, whereas M. reticulata flowers later, from March to May. The species is also recognised by the distinctive cataphylls, the uppermost of which extends well above the ground as a grey or brown basket-like network around the base of the leaf and stem. Occasionally also seen in M. spathulata, the cataphylls are never as prominently developed.

claims.text: Distinguished among the yellow-flowered species of subg. Homeria by the solitary, broad, glaucous leaf, the lower portion clasping the stem, and the half to fully pendent flowers with reflexed tepal limbs. The tips of the tepal claws clasp the thickened filament column but are slightly bowed toward the bases, which contain nectar. The style branches are relatively well developed and bear broad stigmatic lobes and straight linear crests. Moraea reflexa may be confused with superficially similar M. marlothii, a taller, more robust species that occurs widely across the western Karoo, but the tepals in that species, either yellow or pink, spread horizontally or are sometimes half reflexed, the filament column is usually narrow and cylindric or only slightly thickened below, and the ovary is long and slender and curved outward, whereas the shorter ovary of M. reflexa is straight, top-shaped and widest near the apex. Although the flowers of M. marlothii are comparable in size to those of M. reflexa, it has much larger anthers 8-11 mm long compared with anthers ± 6 mm long in M. reflexa.

claims.text: One of the taller species in the genus, plants often exceeding 1 m in height, and exhibits such ancestral features as multiple foliage leaves and an unspecialised yellow flower. Notably the filaments are free or barely united at the base, evidently a derived condition. Peculiar to the species are the hard, spiny roots that enclose the corm and hundreds of cormlets produced around the base. The spiny roots probably have a protective function but they evidently do not prevent massive depredation by baboons and porcupines that uproot large numbers of plants in search of the edible corms. The survival of such populations is assured by the production of cormlets which are shed in large numbers from the base of the main corm and also from the lower aerial nodes. The corm tunics, often decayed at flowering, consist of firm, leathery, brown layers that split from the base.

claims.text: Resembling Moraea unguiculata, M. rivulicola has larger, pale, creamy green, yellow-green or beige flowers, the outer tepals up to 28 mm long with limbs typically held at 60° below horizontal and smooth claws. The inner tepals are also distinctive in having the central lobe of the typically 3-lobed limb drawn into a slender, obliquely coiled cusp, while the lateral lobes are rounded and very short. The ovary is oblong-cylindric and 11-14 mm long, and gives rise to large cylindric capsules 25-32 mm long. Moraea unguiculata has smaller flowers with the outer tepals seldom exceeding 16 mm and with densely pubescent or bearded claws. The inner tepals, 7-10 mm long, are also 3-lobed but the long central cusp is coiled inward symmetrically. Flower colour in M. unguiculata ranges from white to creamy white, brownish, and even blue, and the outer tepal limbs may be half reflexed or, in some populations outside Namaqualand, may be completely reflexed. A population from the rocky hills west of Bitterfontein and south of Kotzesrus stands out in the particularly large flowers with the inner tepals ± 19 mm long, and with an ovate-attenuate limb. Other organs are also larger, with the filaments united in a column up to 10 mm long and free for an additional 2.5 mm and the anthers are 5.5-6.0 mm long. This population represents a significant variant and distinctive race, perhaps deserving of infraspecific recognition.

claims.text: Recognised by the solitary foliage leaf inserted well above the ground, sparsely branched (rarely simple), flexuose stem, and yellow flower with the erect tepal claws forming a narrow cup ± 10 mm long completely enclosing the stamens. The filaments are entirely united in a cylindric column 4-5 mm long relatively densely hairy in the lower half, and the anthers, 5-8 mm long, are usually slightly shorter than the style branches. The nearly erect style branches, ± 5 mm long, bear short, horizontal crests, hardly visible in pressed flowers. Moraea pyrophila may be most closely related to M. autumnalis, which has the foliage leaf inserted close to ground level, and deeper yellow flowers with a floral cup including the filaments and only the bases of the anthers. Moraea pyrophila may also be confused with M. collina but that species has a longer leaf, usually trailing distally in contrast to the very short, apically thickened leaf of M. pyrophila, which seldom exceeds the stem.

claims.text: Resembling the more common and widespread Moraea crispa in both flower structure and general aspect, M. pseudospicata has pale blue-mauve flowers with subequal tepals with short erect claws that form a short, narrow cup including the lower part of the filament column. The anthers are nearly erect and so concealing the narrow and short style branches, whereas in M. crispa the anthers and style branches diverge, exposing the style branches. Moraea pseudospicata differs also in its taller stature, up to 400 mm high, sessile lateral inflorescences with dry, chaffy sheathing leaves and rhipidial spathes, and in its globose capsules with almost membranous walls, apparently dehiscing irregularly rather than along the locule sutures. Flowering middle to late summer in an area of summer drought, the leaves are usually dry and broken at flowering time.

claims.text: Moraea margaretae has the brown, ± woody corm tunics, leathery rhipidial spathes with brown tips and flowers with finely brown-veined yellow tepals characteristic of subg. Umbellatae, and is distinguished in the subgenus by its habit and flowers with well-developed style branches and prominent style crests. The leaves and branches (when present) are crowded close to ground level and the aerial stem and branches comprise a single internode. The species is tetraploid, 2n = 40 (two populations counted), one of the few exclusively polyploid species known in Moraea. Moraea margaretae seems to be most closely related to M. orthrosantha of central Namaqualand but this species has aerial stems of three or four internodes, with two or three branches at the aerial nodes. The flowers of the two are similar in size and colour but those of M. margaretae have shorter filaments ± 5 mm long vs. filaments 8-9 mm long in M. orthrosantha. Both species have red anthers and pollen. Hybrids between M. margaretae and M. intermedia occur at a site west of Springbok.

claims.text: Plants 150-200 mm high. Corm unknown. Stem mostly 2- to 4-branched, flexed above sheaths of basal and cauline leaves, sheathing leaves 30-40 mm long, attenuate, dry and light brown in distal half. Foliage leaf solitary, basal, linear, falcate, ± twice as long as stem, narrowly channelled, ± 2 mm wide opened flat, often dry and trailing distally. Rhipidial spathes dry and light brown in distal half, attenuate, inner 30-35 mm long, outer almost half as long. Flowers fugaceous, pale ivory-yellow, limbs of all tepals with deeper yellow nectar guides at bases, spreading; outer tepals narrowly obovate, 20-25 x 7-8 mm, limbs 18-22 mm long, claws of both whorls ± 2 mm long, ascending as a narrow cup including lower half of filament column, inner tepals 18-21 x 6-7 mm. Filaments ± 5 mm long, united in smooth, cylindric column 4 mm long, free and diverging in upper 1 mm; anthers ± 3 mm long before anthesis, ± 2 mm after releasing pollen, exceeding style branches, yellow; pollen yellow. Ovary spindle-shaped, usually exserted, ± 5.5 mm long; style branches flattened, 2.5 x 1.5 mm long, with broad stigmatic lobes, crests ± linear, erect, ± 1 mm long. Capsules obovoid, ± 10 mm long. Seeds unknown.

claims.text: Known only from the Farm Vleiland in the northern foothills of the Klein Swartberg Mtns in Western Cape, South Africa; on clay slopes. Diagnosis: the relatively small, pale yellow flowers of Moraea eburnea have moderately well-developed, flattened style branches terminating in unusually broad stigmatic lobes and short, erect crests somewhat unusual in subg. claims.text: Virtually identical to the relatively common Moraea stricta in vegetative features and life history, M. thomsonii is distinguished only by the flowers. The blue-mauve tepals have nectar guides on both the outer and inner tepal limbs and the inner tepals, ± 7 mm wide, are broader than in M. stricta. The style branches are poorly developed and have vestigial crests shorter than the stigma lobes. In M. stricta the style crests are 3-4 mm long and held erect above the nectar guides and the inner tepals are only 3-4 mm wide. As in M. stricta, the leaf is terete, usually dry and broken at flowering time and the sheathing leaves and spathes are more-or-less dry.

claims.text: The growth habit, corm tunics, characteristic branching with sticky internodes, and the free but parallel and coherent filaments all place Moraea simplex firmly in subg. Visciramosae but its simple filiform, apically stigmatic style branches extending outward between the top of the filaments, and short, suberect tepals claws ± 2 mm long are unique in the subgenus and remarkable in Moraea, in which just two species of subg. Polyanthes have similar style branches. claims.text: Like its apparent close relative, Moraea galpinii, M. robusta has distinctive coarsely fibrous corm tunics forming a collar around the stem base but it differs from M. galpinii in its larger, white or pale yellow flowers with the limbs of both the inner and outer tepals at length spreading to laxly reflexed, the outer tepals 55-65 mm long vs. ± 40 mm in M. galpinii. The leaf is channelled and wider than in M. galpinii, 4-10 mm wide but in some populations the margins are closely inrolled. Populations on the slopes of The Sentinel in the northern KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg have the upper portion dry and broken suggesting emergence before winter, whereas the lower portions are green, evidently having emerged in the spring. The narrowly ellipsoid capsules are up to 45 mm long and up to 10 mm at the widest. The capsules contain numerous angular seeds arranged in two rows per locule. The narrow capsules with a prominent beak and angular seeds stand in marked contrast to the ± ovoid capsules and flattened, discoid seeds of M. spathulata and other species of the subgenus for which these characters are known.

claims.text: With yellow flowers typical of sect. Hexaglottis, Moraea riparia is distinctive largely in its small obovoid to club-shaped capsules and comparatively slender, often willowy stems. The capsules, 6-10 mm long (occasionally up to 12 mm long in robust plants), recall those of M. longifolia but this species has much larger capsules, usually 16-23 mm long. Moraea riparia is diploid, 2n = 12, whereas M. longifolia, usually a taller plant, is tetraploid, 2n = 24. The flowers of M. riparia are deep yellow and scented in contrast to the pale yellow, usually odourless flowers of M. longifolia.
