claims.text: Although vegetatively resembling several other species of sect. Homeria in the solitary, somewhat glaucous leaf inserted above the ground and the few-branched stem, Moraea radians is so distinctive in its floral structures that it was at first referred to a separate genus, Sessilistigma. The beige-yellow flowers, with short, erect tepal claws and spreading limbs, are remarkable for the subgenus in their free stamens and almost vestigial style ± 1 mm long, dividing into three, flattened branches forked for half their length. Other species of subg. Homeria have filaments partly to entirely united and enclosing a well-developed style, the branches of which are each appressed to the opposed anther. The style branches of M. radians lack crests and are stigmatic at the tips of each lobe.

claims.text: Plants 70-150 mm high. Corms 12-15 mm diam.; tunics wiry, dark brown, accumulating in a dense mass, becoming finely netted distally. Stem simple or 1- or 2-branched, branches usually shortly emerging from subtending sheathing leaf, ascending, bearing ± dry, attenuate sheathing leaves ± 20 mm long. Foliage leaf solitary, usually slightly longer than stem, channelled to ± flat, mostly 3-5 mm wide, laxly twisted, trailing to ± prostrate, margins pale, thickened, undulate to crisped. Rhipidial spathes becoming dry at flowering time, often lacerated, inner 25-30 mm long, outer ± 2/3 as long. Flowers fugaceous, pale blue-mauve to almost white, outer tepal limbs with large yellow nectar guides with white centre at bases, half reflexed; outer tepals 22-28 x ± 12 mm, limbs 15-18 mm long, claws 8-10 mm long (thus ± half as long as limbs); inner tepals 18-25 x ± 5 mm, limbs ultimately half reflexed. Filaments 8-9 mm long, united in lower half; anthers 3.5-5.0 mm long, pale mauve; pollen white. Ovary narrowly ellipsoid, ± 7 mm long, included; style branches ± 7.5 mm long, crests 8-12 mm long, lanceolate. Capsules ± ellipsoid, 8-9 mm long, with beak ± 1 mm long. Seeds unknown.

claims.text: With a solitary, twisted and trailing leaf with undulate to crisped margins, Moraea quartzicola appears to be closely allied to the Namaqualand species M. saxicola but is distinguished by its smaller stature, up to 150 mm high, and smaller spathes and flowers, the outer tepals 22-24 mm long with short claws 8-10 mm long, the limbs thus almost twice as long. Moraea saxicola, always a taller plant, rarely < 250 mm high, has inner rhipidial spathes 40-60 mm long (vs. 25-30 mm), and outer tepals 30-40 mm long with the claws about as long as the limbs. Other floral parts of M. saxicola are likewise larger that those of M. quartzicola.

claims.text: Up to 600 mm tall, Moraea pubiflora is a fairly robust species of sect. Vieusseuxia and most easily distinguished by inner tepals divided into 3 subequal slender, spreading, brown-speckled lobes, the outer two expanded at the tips and obtuse, and the inner slender with a ± acute apex and curving upward distally. The outer tepal limbs are typically white but the claws, inner tepals and style branches and crests are densely dotted with dark brown on a pale yellow to greenish background. A particularly unusual feature of the species is the scabrid to velvety surface of the outside of the outer tepals. Similar in flower structure, although smooth or papillate on the outside of the outer tepals, M. brevistyla has similarly coloured but much smaller flowers, the outer tepals 18-20 mm long and the filaments just 5-7 mm long compared with outer tepals 25-30 mm long and filaments 13-15 mm long in M. pubiflora.

claims.text: Widespread and relatively common in interior southern Africa, Moraea polystachya is recognised by the combination of several foliage leaves, branched stem, and large blue-mauve to violet flowers. The limbs of both tepal whorls are half reflexed but only the outer tepals bear nectar guides, and the tepal claws form a narrow cup enclosing the filaments and broad style branches, leaving the style crests prominently displayed. An unusual and particularly distinctive feature of most populations is the red veining on the ovary, this absent in plants from the Little Karoo. Once regarded as an ecological variant of M. polystachya, M. venenata is now regarded as a separate, but closely related species. A shorter plant, M. venenata has somewhat larger flowers with inner tepals usually held ± erect, the ovary also typically red-veined. The larger capsules, up to 16-20 mm long, are nodding when mature and contain larger seeds, ± 2 mm long. Capsules of M. polystachya are held erect, are 9-16 mm long and the smaller seeds are 1.2-1.6 mm long. Both M. polystachya and M. venenata are poisonous to stock. Moraea polystachya in the Little Karoo is distinctive not only in lacking red veining on the ovary but in having blue rather than violet flowers with the inner tepals held erect for most of the flowering cycle. No other features appear to distinguish these plants, which flower in the winter months rather than in late summer and autumn.

claims.text: Recognised by the branched stem bearing two to four foliage leaves, and moderate-sized, blue to blue-mauve, violet or rarely white flowers with style branches as narrow and as long as or slightly longer than the anthers and lacking style crests. The ascending tepal claws diverge slightly to form a relatively narrow cup that includes the filaments and the lower part of the anthers or all of the anthers, and the tepal limbs spread more-or-less horizontally. The filaments are united in a slender, smooth column usually 7-9 mm long. A notable variant of the species from near Albertinia and Herbertsdale in southern Western Cape has slightly smaller, white or pale blue flowers with the filaments only 5-6 mm long, and both filaments and anthers are included in the floral cup whereas the anthers are usually fully excluded from the cup in typical M. polyanthos. The species is closely allied to M. bipartita, which has conventional Moraea-type flowers with broad style branches with prominent crests but the two are identical in vegetative features. Hybrids between these two species have been recorded where they co-occur.

claims.text: Readily recognised by its small, predominantly white flowers with outer tepals up to 27 mm long, and dark purple style branches and crests, Moraea modesta is a low-growing species, seldom reaching more than 200 mm in height. The vestigial inner tepals are 5-6 mm long, either hair-like cusps or obscurely 3-lobed at the apex. It is one of several species that flower after the foliage leaf, produced the previous summer, is dry and dead. The leaf is sometimes retained at flowering, still attached to the base of the flowering stem but more often has decayed and is no longer evident. A new, emergent leaf is sometimes present at flowering, extending well above the stem later in the growing season. Populations from near Machadodorp in central Mpumalanga have more-or-less free filaments, unusual for the species, and require additional study. In other populations the filaments are united for at least half their length.

claims.text: Flowering in mid-winter in May and June, Moraea longipes has the general aspect of M. ciliata and M. tricolor except that the stem is not subterranean at flowering but extends up to 180 mm above ground. Like most species of subg. Acaules the ovary is retracted to the base of the inflorescence spathes after flowering. The flowers are most like those of M. ciliata but have slightly broader style crests, triangular with the base 2.5-3.0 mm wide (± linear in M. ciliata) and the filaments are united basally for ± 1.5 mm, about one fifth of their length, as are those of most other species of subg. Acaules. The anthers of M. longipes are the longest in the subgenus, 7.5-9.0 mm long (5-8 mm in M. ciliata) and are held above the nectar guides on filaments as long as the tepal claws. A notable feature of M. longipes is the collar of fibres around the underground part of the stem, uncommon but not unique in the subgenus. The species flowers early in the season, May to early July, and grows in places where M. ciliata has been found in bloom six to eight weeks later. Flower colour in M. longipes is either pale, watery yellow or translucent white, then with the edges of the outer tepal limbs and the inner tepal limbs a pale coppery pink colour and with the tepals flushed the same colour outside.

claims.text: Allied to the well-known and widespread Moraea ciliata and occurring entirely within the range of this species, M. macronyx can be distinguished by its larger flowers with the outer tepal claws one and a half to twice as long as the limbs. The larger outer tepals are 40-60 mm long with the claws 25-40 mm long and the style branches are ± 20 mm long with crests up to 25 mm long. The outer tepals of M. ciliata are mostly 25-35 mm long with the claws 12-15 mm long, thus about half as long as the limbs, and the style branches are typically 8-15 mm long. Vegetatively M. macronyx and M. ciliata are nearly identical although the corm tunics may differ, those of M. macronyx sometimes unusual in being entire and peculiarly soft, of an almost spongy, pith-like texture. Some populations, however, have fibrous corm tunics no different from those of M. ciliata.

claims.text: Distinguished by its robust, several- to many-branched stem and characteristic flowers with the tepal claws widely diverging to form a shallow dish including the filaments and bases of the anthers. The tepals are usually salmon-pink with a yellow cup but populations with uniformly yellow flowers are not uncommon. When dry the shape of the flowers is often lost but its large size makes identification fairly easy. The tepals, ovary, filaments, anthers, and capsules are amongst the largest in the genus. The outer tepals are usually 35-40 mm long, and the filaments are ± 8 mm long with the anthers up to 11 mm long. The ovary, initially 17-20 mm long, elongates after fertilization and the capsules may reach a length of 55 mm. The capsules are notable in having a pointed beak some 2 mm long. Earlier-flowering Moraea collina has been confused in the past with M. flaccida but is a shorter, few-branched species, the flowers with suberect tepal claws forming a narrow cup enclosing both filaments and anthers. The tepals of M. collina seldom exceed 35 mm, the filaments are 6-7 mm long, and the anthers are slightly shorter, 5?6 mm long. The ovary in M. collina is often as long as that of M. flaccida and the capsule may attain a length of over 35 mm. Capsules of M. collina, however, have a shorter, rather obtuse beak ± 1 mm long. Although M. flaccida flowers relatively late in the season, by which time M. collina is usually in fruit, their flowering times may overlap and natural hybrids have been recorded between the two species on the Cape Peninsula.

claims.text: Closely resembling Moraea fugax in general appearance except smaller in all features, M. filicaulis has a slender, almost filiform stem ± 1 mm in diam., and one or more often two subequal or unequal, filiform, narrowly channelled leaves inserted at the first above ground internode. The flowers are usually white, but occasionally pink or blue-mauve or even violet, and have outer tepals mostly 20-35 mm long (occasionally longer) and inner tepals 18-30 mm long. Flowers of M. fugax have outer tepals mostly 30-45 mm long and inner tepals 25-35 mm long. The inner rhipidial spathes, a useful measure of plant size, are 20-35(-40) mm long in M. filicaulis but 40-65 mm long in M. fugax. Moraea filicaulis has been treated as a subspecies of M. fugax and an important reason for recognising it as a separate species is that it sometimes co-occurs with typical M. fugax but always showing slightly different habitat preferences.

claims.text: Cormous geophyte, up to 250 mm tall, stem few-branched. Leaf solitary, linear, channelled, inserted shortly above ground. Flowers pale blue-lilac, outer tepals with bright orange marks near limb bases, tepals unequal, with long, narrow ascending claws, inner much smaller, limbs slightly reflexed, filaments in a long, slender column, style crests well developed, opening late afternoon, lasting until late evening. Mainly Oct.

claims.text: Although vegetatively there is little to distinguish Moraea macgregoriorum from related species, including M. saxicola and it allies, in the solitary, rather narrow undulate leaf, branched stem and ± dry spathes, the flower is, however, striking: the pale blue-lilac tepals are held well apart from one another and have long, very narrow claws, narrow, spreading to reflexed limbs and characteristic orange nectar guides. Particularly distinctive are the elongate filaments ± 15 mm long and disproportionately short anthers ± 4 mm long (M. saxicola has filaments 12-14 mm long and anthers 6-9 mm long). As in other members of sect. Deserticolae the ovary is included in the spathes. Molecular phylogenetic studies show that M. macgregoriorum is closely allied to M. saxicola and M. bolusii.
